new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's tonal coding and with the existing Downing & Nilsson 2019 statement that H is culminative on the penult or final mora and positioned by morphology; it adds that these 'accentual' restrictions hold for roots but are synchronically violated in progressive verb forms, and it explicitly disputes the one-H-per-Phonological-Word wordhood diagnostic used by Downing & Nilsson (2019), Le Gac (2002), Green & Morrison (2016, 2018), saying the rule 'is not synchronically productive' in Central-Northern Somali (pp. 587-588, 595). Describes Northern Somali (Northwestern + Benaadir = Central-Northern, and the post-1972 koiné), p. 589.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Somali (Northern group) is a tone language with a privative H vs. toneless contrast; every root carries at most one High tone, on the final or penultimate mora (only vowels are moraic; final = feminine, penultimate = masculine in the gender-marking declension). Footnote 3 (p. 590) explicitly follows Hyman in treating Somali as a tone system with distributional restrictions rather than as a stress or 'accent' type. The authors argue that in Central-Northern Somali these word-level restrictions have been weakened by grammaticalization: progressive verb forms have the H 'too far' from the right edge (keénayaa) or two H tones (keénayó), so the synchronic system is 'morphological tone' tied to constructions, not to a word domain.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not applicable (no stress; nothing on secondary prominence). Two H tones per word occur in negative progressive forms (keénayó), which the authors treat as a breach of culminativity, not as secondary prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: Toneless words exist (wada 'together', kala 'apart', many verb forms), so H is not obligatory. Progressive forms keénayaa / keénayó (H not at the right edge; two H tones) violate demarcativity and culminativity; explained diachronically from *keéni hayaa. Northeastern Somali and Maay are said to retain more archaic patterns (Maay variation sheenә háayaan ~ sheenáayaan, citing Saeed 1999).
new_statements.identity_note: Kaldhol & Stausland Johnsen 2021 describe Northern Somali, specifically Central-Northern Somali (Northwestern + Benaadir, Tosco 2012's term) and the post-1972 spoken koiné, checked with native speakers in San Diego and Oslo; they note Northeastern Somali and Maay retain more archaic tone patterns. Salt 1814's 'Somauli' vocabulary comes from a single northern-coast informant with no dialect stated.

tone_statements.quote: Since the seminal study of Hyman (1981), Somali is generally considered a tonal- or pitch-accent language. Tonal accent (TA) consists of a phonological high tone, realized as a high or mid pitch target. This pitch target is associated with an intensity peak, which is referred to either as 'stress' (e.g. Armstrong 1934, Andrzejewski 1964, Orwin 1995) or 'accent' (Hyman 1981; Banti 1988; Saeed 1999; Le Gac 2001, 2003a, b among others). Syllable duration is not a phonetic correlate of TA. The TA-bearing unit is the vocalic mora. There is at most one TA per word, which occurs either on the penultimate or on the last mora of the word. TA is not lexically distinctive but determined by various grammatical features such as gender, number, case, verb inflection etc.

readall_conflicts: One substantive disagreement among the sources, not with the catalog's classification: Kaldhol & Stausland Johnsen 2021 accept the descriptive generalisation that a Somali root has at most one High tone on its final or penultimate mora (the same placement recorded from Downing & Nilsson 2019), but they deny that culminativity and demarcativity hold synchronically at the word level in Central-Northern Somali, arguing from progressive verb forms (keénayaa, keénayó) that the H is now morphological tone attached to constructions and that the 'one H per (Phonological) Word' rule used by Downing & Nilsson (2019), Le Gac (2002) and Green & Morrison (2016, 2018) as a wordhood diagnostic 'is not synchronically productive'. Both sides agree Somali is tonal rather than stress-accented. Salt 1814 is silent.

sources.quote: Since the seminal study of Hyman (1981), Somali is generally considered a tonal- or pitch-accent language. Tonal accent (TA) consists of a phonological high tone, realized as a high or mid pitch target. This pitch target is associated with an intensity peak, which is referred to either as 'stress' (e.g. Armstrong 1934, Andrzejewski 1964, Orwin 1995) or 'accent' (Hyman 1981; Banti 1988; Saeed 1999; Le Gac 2001, 2003a, b among others). Syllable duration is not a phonetic correlate of TA. The TA-bearing unit is the vocalic mora. There is at most one TA per word, which occurs either on the penultimate or on the last mora of the word. TA is not lexically distinctive but determined by various grammatical features such as gender, number, case, verb inflection etc.
